newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to permit bond stripping from middle 1997.
newsitem.headline: Germany to permit bond stripping from middle 1997.

text.p: The German government on Friday unveiled a key change in the way its debt can be traded, bringing it into line with international standards and further improving Germany's status as a leading financial centre.

In a long awaited move, the Bundesbank said Germany would allow bond dealers to strip 10- and 30-year bonds from July 1997. This means the bond can be split into its principal and its coupon. The two are then sold separately, the principal as zero-coupon securities.

Although the Bonn government and the central bank have mulled the issue of permitting bond-stripping for several years, it was the spectre of European currency union that likely helped spur the final decision.
"Germany did this for Europe," said Heinz Gunasekera, bond analyst at UBS in Frankfurt.
While the step is likely to appeal to only a limited audience, analysts said it was one of many small steps taken in Germany recently to overhaul the financial market.

"This won't take the market hugely forward. But the number of small steps, like the Finance Ministry now issuing debt across the yield curve, all move in one direction," giving the German market new sophistication, said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.
Beside improving the German market's image, the step is also seen as giving bankers some hands-on training with new products in the run-up to Europe's planned currency union.

"This step is absolutely necessary to help Germany reach an international standard and give banks experience in dealing with this business before Europe's currency union is slated to begin," said Armin Kayser, analyst at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt.

The Bundesbank said Bonn would issue a strippable 30-year bond in the middle of the year which it plans to top up later. Both the government's already issued 6.25 percent bond maturing 2024 and the New Year bond for 1997 would also be strippable, the Bundesbank said.

Kayser and others predicted that bond-stripping will be permitted in the currency union, particularly since the practice has become hugely popular in many nations since being pioneered by U.S. investment banks several years ago.
For banks the most attractive aspect of bond-stripping, which effectively allows dealers to trade the same product twice, may be that arbitrage opportunities will be increased.
Here dealers can profit from differences in price when the same security is traded on two or more markets.

After complaining that the German market suffered a distinct competitive disadvantage when stripping was prohibited, commercial banks cheered today's news, which delivered what the government had promised since the summer.
Stephan Schuster, a senior official at Deutsche Bank said: "Of course we welcome this, in fact it was one of the demands we made" in discussions with the government and Bundesbank.
The Bundesbank acts as the government's issuing agent.
One reason it may have taken so long for the practice to be officially approved is that Bonn long struggled with a myriad of thorny tax issues pertaining to the issues.
The Finance Ministry said certain technical issues still needed to be worked out, and this was a reason stripping will not become effective until the middle of next year.

While the step is seen helping the German market, if only in a small way, SBC Warburg's Kayser criticised the timing, saying: "There is no reason to be jubilant about this move as it comes so late in the game."
Europe's currency union is due to begin on January 1, 1999.
